q: Which of these measures the spread of a data set rather than its centre?
x: The range (largest value minus smallest) shows how spread out the data is. Mean, median and mode are all measures of the centre (central tendency).

q: A survey asks 300 students, chosen from all 12,000 students of a university, about their study hours. The 300 students form:
x: The population is the whole group of interest (all 12,000 students); the 300 chosen from it are a sample. A control group belongs to an experiment, not a survey.

q: Marks: 6, 9, 3, 9, 8. What are the mean, median and mode, in that order?
x: Mean = 35 / 5 = 7. Sorted: 3, 6, 8, 9, 9, so the median is 8; 9 occurs twice, so the mode is 9. 3 is the middle value before sorting, not the median.

q: The mean of the four numbers 5, 8, x and 11 is 9. What is x?
x: The four numbers must add up to 4 × 9 = 36; 5 + 8 + 11 = 24, so x = 36 − 24 = 12. 36 is the total, not the missing number.

q:
What is printed?
```
data = [3, 8, 3, 5, 8, 3]
print(max(data) - min(data), data.count(3))
```
x: max − min = 8 − 3 = 5 (the range), and 3 appears three times, so `count(3)` is 3. 8 is the largest value alone, not the range.

q: A model scores 99% accuracy on the data it was trained on but only 60% on new test data. What does this most likely show?
o: It needs to be tested on its training data only
It has overfitted: it fits the training data too closely and does not generalise
The test data must be wrong, so the test should be ignored
It is the best possible model, since training accuracy matters most
x: A model that does very well on its training data but much worse on unseen data has learnt the training examples rather than the general pattern: overfitting. Evaluation on unseen test data is exactly what reveals this.

q: In an experiment on a revision app, students are put into the app group or the no-app group at random, for example by drawing names. Why is this done?
o: So the app group always gets the stronger students
So the two groups are alike, and a difference in scores can be put down to the app
So that no control group is needed
So the results can be found without collecting data
x: Random assignment spreads students' abilities evenly between the groups, so the only planned difference is the app. Choosing stronger students for one group would bias the result.

q: Every value in a data set is increased by 5. What happens to the mean and to the range?
o: The mean stays the same; the range increases by 5
The mean increases by 5; the range stays the same
x: Adding 5 to each value adds 5 to their total over n values, so the mean rises by 5. The largest and smallest values both rise by 5, so their difference, the range, does not change. Example: 2, 4, 9 → 7, 9, 14.

q: A model predicts house prices (in lakh rupees). For three houses the actual prices are 40, 50 and 60 and the predicted prices are 43, 48 and 61. What is the mean absolute error (the average size of the errors, ignoring their signs)?
x: Errors ignoring sign: |43 − 40| = 3, |48 − 50| = 2, |61 − 60| = 1; their mean is 6 / 3 = 2. 0.67 keeps the signs (3 − 2 + 1 = 2, then 2 / 3), which lets errors cancel; 6 is the total, not the mean.

q: In a class, 10 students have an average mark of 60 and the other 30 students have an average mark of 80. What is the average mark of the whole class?
x: Total marks = 10 × 60 + 30 × 80 = 600 + 2,400 = 3,000 for 40 students, so the mean is 3,000 / 40 = 75. 70, the average of 60 and 80, ignores that the second group is three times larger.

q: Which chart best compares the number of students enrolled in five different departments of a college?
x: A bar chart compares amounts across separate categories such as departments. A line chart suits change over time, and a histogram shows how a numeric variable is spread over ranges.

q: The marks of 200 students are grouped into the ranges 0–20, 21–40, 41–60, 61–80 and 81–100, and the number of students in each range is drawn as touching bars. What is this chart called?
x: A histogram shows how often values fall into consecutive numeric ranges, with bars that touch. A pie chart shows shares of one whole, and a scatter plot shows pairs of values.

q: A sales file stores prices as text, such as "Rs 1,200" and "Rs 950". What should data cleaning do before the average price is worked out?
o: Delete the price column, since text cannot be averaged
Remove the "Rs" and the commas and convert the values to numbers
Replace every price with the most common price
x: Cleaning puts each column into the right format: prices must be numbers before they can be averaged. Deleting the column or replacing values would throw away real data.

q: A bar chart shows two shops' sales of 92 and 96 units, but its vertical axis starts at 90 instead of 0, so one bar looks three times as tall as the other. What is wrong with the chart?
o: It should be a pie chart, because there are only two values
It exaggerates a small difference and can mislead readers
Nothing; the axis may start at any value without changing the picture
The two bars should be in the same colour
x: With the axis starting at 90 the bars show 2 and 6, so a 4-unit gap (about 4%) looks like a threefold difference. Starting a bar chart's axis at 0 keeps the bar heights in proportion.

q: In hypothesis testing, which hypothesis is tested directly and is either rejected or not rejected?
x: The test measures the evidence against H₀, which is then rejected or not rejected. H₁ is accepted only indirectly, when H₀ is rejected.

q: A test of a new teaching method gives p = 0.002. What does this small p-value mean?
o: There is a 0.2% chance that the method works
The sample was too small to use
A result like this would be very unlikely if H₀ were true, so it is strong evidence against H₀
x: The p-value is the chance of getting a result at least this extreme if H₀ were true; 0.002 is tiny, so H₀ is doubtful. It is not the chance that the method works.

q: Which of these is a testable hypothesis?
o: Students who sleep 8 hours score higher on average than students who sleep 5 hours
x: A hypothesis is a statement that can be checked with data, here by comparing two groups' average scores. A question is not a hypothesis, and opinions such as "sleep is wonderful" cannot be measured.

q: Four studies test their null hypotheses at α = 0.05 and get the p-values 0.20, 0.04, 0.07 and 0.009. In how many studies is H₀ rejected?
x: H₀ is rejected when p < α: 0.04 and 0.009 are below 0.05, while 0.20 and 0.07 are not. So 2 studies reject H₀; 0.07 is close but still above 0.05.
